89	### Conclusion C1: The reported doubling of quarterly churn is not yet a validated behavioral signal — it may be partly or wholly an artifact of which renewal cohort fell in each quarter, and resolving this must precede trusting the headline number
90	
91	GT-1 (Q1 ratio 4.1%) + GT-2 (Q3 ratio 9.2%) + GT-3 (annual, yearly-renewing contracts) + GT-10 (no cohort data supplied)
92	→ because churn is only realized at each contract's renewal date, a quarterly churn percentage on an annually-renewing book is the loss ratio among the specific cohort whose renewal fell due that quarter, not a rate applied continuously across the whole book
93	→ that renewal-due cohort's size and composition can differ from quarter to quarter, so a rise in the ratio is consistent with either a real rise in per-customer churn propensity or a shift in which cohort happened to renew that quarter
94	→ no cohort-size or cohort-composition data has been pulled (confirmed directly by GT-10), so the 4.1%→9.2% comparison cannot yet be read as a confirmed behavioral rate change — it is equally consistent with a renewal-cohort artifact until that data is pulled
95	
96	**Confidence:** HIGH — every hop follows by deduction from GT-3's contract mechanics (A-8) and GT-10's confirmed data absence; the rival reading ("the doubling is already a confirmed real change") is ruled out by the endpoint itself, which establishes that no data yet exists to confirm it either way — the endpoint is itself the rival-ruling move, so the Rivals axis is satisfied rather than left open.
97	
98	### Conclusion C2: On a naive persistence-based annualization, both the pre-spike and spike quarters imply an annual-equivalent churn rate above the published "weak" threshold for mid-market B2B SaaS — the Q3 spike is likely an acceleration of an existing problem, not a new one — but this bracket rests on an unverified persistence/uniformity assumption
99	
100	GT-1 (Q1 ratio 4.1%) + GT-2 (Q3 ratio 9.2%) + GT-9 (mid-market benchmark bands: >12% Weak, 7-12% Healthy, <7% Best-in-class)
101	→ compounding each quarterly ratio across four quarters as if it persisted unchanged brackets the implied annual-equivalent churn between about 15.4 percent (from Q1's 4.1%, since 1 − 0.959⁴ ≈ 0.154) and about 32.0 percent (from Q3's 9.2%, since 1 − 0.908⁴ ≈ 0.320) *[Assumes: A-11 — a single quarter's ratio approximates steady-state annual behavior]*
102	→ even the lower, pre-spike end of that bracket (about 15.4 percent) already sits above GT-9's Weak threshold (above 12 percent) for mid-market annual logo churn
103	→ this suggests Northbrook's book was already running in weak-performance territory before Q3's acceleration, not that Q3 marks the onset of a previously healthy book
104	
105	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — the Inference axis is short: the first hop rests on [Assumes: A-11], and if cohort composition is not stable or representative across quarters (exactly what chain C1 flags as unconfirmed), the true annualized figure could differ substantially from this bracket in either direction — A-11's failure has not been shown to leave the endpoint unaffected. Verification: pull actual trailing-12-month cohort-weighted churn once A-1/A-2 renewal-cohort data exists; that measurement supersedes this proxy bracket entirely.
106	
107	### Conclusion C3: The two CS-flagged symptoms are more likely common effects of a single upstream change than two independent problems, but this rests on an unverified timing assumption and a live, unruled-out independent-causes rival
108	
109	GT-5 (ticket volume up) + GT-6 (adoption score down) + GT-7 (no cause confirmed yet)
110	→ absent ticket-category, time-to-resolution, and adoption-methodology data, the two symptoms' co-occurrence in the same roughly two-quarter window is more parsimoniously explained by one dated upstream event than by two unrelated processes independently drifting in the same direction at the same time *[Assumes: A-3 — the symptoms and the churn rise are not independently timed]*
111	→ of the plausible common-upstream events, an onboarding or time-to-value degradation dated roughly two to three quarters before Q3 best fits the lag structure, since the annual-renewal mechanic (GT-3, A-8) means a cohort onboarded poorly in late Q4 or Q1 would generate how-to tickets and depressed adoption immediately but would not surface as churn until that cohort's own renewal lands in Q2 or Q3
112	→ this is the leading inference, not a demonstrated fact — a fully independent-causes account, such as ticket growth from organic usage scale combined with an adoption-score methodology artifact (A-12), remains equally consistent with GT-5 and GT-6 alone and is not yet ruled out
113	
114	**Confidence:** LOW — two axes are short at once. Inference: the second hop rests on [Assumes: A-3], and its failure (the symptoms are not timing-coincidental with the churn rise) would materially weaken the common-cause reading, which has not been priced as leaving the endpoint unaffected. Rivals: the independent-causes rival named in the third hop is live and nothing in this analysis settles it yet (the organic-growth-only sub-case is addressed in Abandoned Reasoning AR-1, but the full rival, including the adoption-score-artifact sub-case, remains open). Verification: a monthly time-series overlay closes A-3; a ticket-category and adoption-methodology audit closes A-12 and bears directly on the rival.
115	
116	### Conclusion C4: Run the four internal, fast, cheap diagnostics in parallel first, gate the costlier pricing and competitive investigation on what that wave shows, assign an independent reviewer to spot-check implicated teams' own data, and set explicit leadership expectation of a multi-quarter lag before a correct fix shows up in the churn number
117	
118	C1 (HIGH, framing confound named) + GT-7 (hypothesis list, non-exhaustive) + GT-8 (same)
119	→ weighing six investigation options (renewal-cohort reconstruction; ticket-category and time-to-resolution breakdown; adoption-score audit; onboarding and time-to-value by cohort; pricing, discount and win-loss or competitor data; doing nothing) against six locked, weighted criteria (framing-confound power ×5, common-cause power ×5, speed ×4, cost and effort ×3, risk-of-being-wrong-if-skipped ×5, hypothesis coverage ×4) scores the four-pull parallel composite highest at 120, ahead of cohort reconstruction alone at 107 and pricing or win-loss data at 55
120	→ the flip test shows no single-criterion reweighting within the 1-5 anchor range changes this ranking, which prices A-13's failure mode directly and leaves the ranking's winner unaffected
121	→ pricing and win-loss or competitor data score lowest on speed and cost because they require cross-functional coordination and qualitative coding, so they are better run as a second, gated wave once the first wave either confirms or rules out the onboarding and service-quality narrative
122	→[2nd] running the first wave asks Support and Product to help characterize data that may implicate their own function, which creates an incentive to under-report, and asks leadership to wait through a diagnostic window during which at-risk accounts already mid-renewal receive no visible fix *[Assumes: A-10 — teams will report completely and without self-protective bias]*
123	→[3rd] because the annual-renewal mechanic (GT-3, A-8) is the same lag that hid the original problem, a correctly identified and fixed root cause will not visibly lower the quarterly churn number for roughly two to three more quarters, so judging the fix by the very next quarter's churn figure risks a premature "it didn't work" verdict and a reversal of a correct intervention
124	
125	No extension step contradicts a Ground Truth (checked against GT-1 through GT-11).
126	
127	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — the Inference axis is short: the fourth hop rests on [Assumes: A-10], and its failure (teams under-report on their own function) is not shown to leave the endpoint unaffected — it would weaken wave-1's reliability, which is exactly why the endpoint already names the independent-reviewer mitigation as a plan change rather than assuming the risk away. Verification: no single observation closes A-10; it is mitigated structurally (independent data pull by a non-implicated reviewer), not resolved by evidence.
128	
129	### Conclusion C5: The "rising tickets plus falling adoption equals service-quality decline caused the churn" narrative is not yet earned and should be carried as the leading hypothesis to test first, not presented as the confirmed root cause
130	
131	GT-5 (ticket volume up) + GT-6 (adoption score down) + GT-7 (no cause confirmed)
132	→ "service-quality decline is the primary driver of the churn spike" would follow only if five load-bearing preconditions all held at once: ticket-rate-per-active-customer, not raw count, has risen; the adoption-score methodology and feature catalog were stable across the window; the churned-logo population overlaps the population whose tickets and adoption were flagged; win/loss reason-coding does not show price or a named competitor as the dominant stated reason; and engagement decline precedes, rather than follows, the renewal decision
133	→ none of these five preconditions is currently verified — A-4 and A-12 leave two of them explicitly open, and GT-10's confirmed data absence leaves the remaining three unverifiable with data this analysis has
134	→ the strong conclusion therefore does not yet follow from the available evidence; it remains the single leading hypothesis among several live ones, not a demonstrated finding
135	
136	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — EXCEPT claimed: this is an absent-fails derivation. If the five named preconditions held, "service-quality decline is the confirmed primary driver" would follow; GT-10 and assumptions A-4/A-12 together establish that those preconditions are unconfirmed, so the strong conclusion does not yet follow. The unconfirmed-precondition set named above is the satisfying evidence for this EXCEPT clause, and the chain remains MEDIUM because it establishes what does not yet follow rather than what does. Verification paths for the individual preconditions are the ones already named under A-4 and A-12.
137	
138	### Conclusion C6: Even under a generous reading of a published "unavoidable churn" heuristic, Northbrook's churn is overwhelmingly not explained by irreducible attrition, but a realistic floor above zero should still be set when judging any intervention's success
139	
140	GT-11? (unavoidable-churn heuristic, roughly 5-10 percent, reported-by-delegate) + GT-1 (Q1 ratio 4.1%) + GT-2 (Q3 ratio 9.2%)
141	→ the governing constraint is that some customer-side business discontinuity — closure, acquisition by a company that consolidates onto its own stack, or budget elimination of the function — occurs across any population of mid-market companies each year, independent of Northbrook's product or service quality
142	→ the cited range in GT-11? is wide and unverified, with other informal sources this analysis has seen suggesting figures as low as 1-3 percent, but even its upper end of 10 percent sits below both of chain C2's annualized brackets of roughly 15.4 percent and 32.0 percent
143	→ this implies the bulk of Northbrook's churn, even at the pre-spike Q1 level, is very unlikely to be fully explained by irreducible, non-addressable attrition — most of it is plausibly addressable, which bounds leadership's expectations without implying churn can be driven to zero
144	
145	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-11? is unverified and reported-by-delegate, carrying a wide and internally inconsistent cited range (5-10 percent vs. an informally-seen 1-3 percent). Verification: pull Northbrook's own CRM "reason for non-renewal" codes for the Q1-Q3 lost logos and tag which are company-dissolution, M&A, or budget-elimination versus a chosen non-renewal — this directly measures Northbrook's own floor rather than relying on an external heuristic.
146	
147	---
148	
149	## 5. Abandoned Reasoning
150	
151	### Dead End: Treating "ticket volume up" as fully explained by organic customer-base growth
152	
153	**What was tried:** Reading the rising ticket count as simply a function of a larger or more active customer base (more seats, more integrations), with no implication of declining service quality.
154	
155	**Why abandoned:** This account cannot stand alone — it does not explain the simultaneous drop in adoption scores (GT-6), and organic growth by itself does not explain a rise in the churn ratio, since growth adds new logos rather than causing existing ones to leave. Chain C3 treats "organic growth" as a possible partial contributing condition, not a complete account, because it fails the counterfactual test for the churn rise specifically.
156	
157	**What it ruled out:** "Pure organic growth, no real problem" as a *complete* explanation for the combined picture (ticket volume up, adoption down, churn up). A partial contributing role for organic growth in the ticket-volume figure specifically is not ruled out and remains a candidate to quantify once ticket-rate-per-active-customer data (A-4's verification) is pulled.
158	
159	### Dead End: Presenting a naive "37% annualized" figure as a confirmed crisis-level finding
160	
161	**What was tried:** Directly multiplying Q3's 9.2% quarterly figure by 4 (9.2 × 4 = 36.8%) and reporting this as Northbrook's confirmed annual churn rate.
162	
163	**Why abandoned:** This is not the correct compounding arithmetic (the estimate procedure in chain C2 recomputes it as 1 − 0.908⁴ ≈ 32.0%, not 36.8%), and more importantly it assumes both persistence and cohort-uniformity across all four quarters — assumptions chain C1 explicitly flags as unverified (A-2, A-11). Presenting either figure as a confirmed finding would overstate certainty this analysis does not have.
164	
165	**What it ruled out:** Nothing about the real world — it ruled out *presenting a single point estimate as fact*. The corrected, explicitly bracketed, explicitly assumption-flagged figure is retained as the upper bound of chain C2's scenario bracket, not as a stand-alone finding.
166	
167	### Dead End: Concluding directly that "service-quality decline" is the confirmed root cause
168	
169	**What was tried:** Taking the intuitively obvious reading of CS's two flagged metrics — rising tickets, falling adoption — as sufficient on its own to confirm that service-quality decline is the primary driver of the churn spike, and moving straight to interventions (more support staff, a win-back campaign) on that basis.
170	
171	**Why abandoned:** The inversion pass (feeding chain C5) found five load-bearing preconditions for this claim, all currently unverified, and chain C3 identified a fully live, unruled-out rival (independent causes, including an adoption-score methodology artifact per A-12). Moving directly to an intervention here risks the premature-intervention failure mode identified in the Phase 5 pre-mortem (Cluster A below).
172	
173	**What it ruled out:** Nothing is yet ruled out by evidence — this entry records that the "clean narrative" was tried and explicitly demoted, by chain C5, from a candidate conclusion to a leading-but-unconfirmed hypothesis pending the five preconditions named there.
174	
175	---
176	
177	## 6. Conclusion
178	
179	**Recommended approach:** Run the four-pronged internal diagnostic wave — renewal-cohort reconstruction, ticket-category and time-to-resolution breakdown, adoption-score audit, and onboarding/time-to-value by cohort — in parallel immediately; gate the pricing and competitive-displacement investigation on what that wave shows; and do not launch a blanket retention or discount intervention until wave-1 findings are in (chain C4).
180	
181	**Key insight:** The 4.1%→9.2% figure cannot yet be read as a clean behavioral signal — annual-contract renewal mechanics mean it may be partly a renewal-cohort artifact (chain C1) — and even on a bracketed, explicitly assumption-flagged annualization, Northbrook's book looks like it was already running in weak-performance territory before Q3's acceleration, not that Q3 marks the onset of a previously healthy book (chain C2); the two CS-flagged symptoms are more likely common effects of one upstream cause, most plausibly an onboarding or time-to-value failure, than two independent problems (chain C3), but the intuitively obvious "service decline caused the churn" story is not yet earned by the evidence available (chain C5).
182	
183	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** Gating the pricing and competitive-displacement investigation behind wave 1 risks losing time if competitive displacement turns out to be the dominant driver (chain C4); the diagnostic plan's criteria weighting reflects analyst judgment rather than a ground-truth-derived measurement, though the flip test shows this specific sequencing choice is robust to reasonable reweighting (chain C4); and leadership should expect any correctly identified fix to lag the churn number by roughly two to three quarters, because of the same annual-contract mechanic that hid the original problem, while accepting that churn cannot be driven to zero — some floor above zero is structurally unavoidable (chain C6).
184	
185	**Confidence:** LOW — the Conclusion's band is capped by chain C3 (LOW), cited for the common-upstream-cause claim in the Key Insight; chains C2, C4, C5, and C6 are each MEDIUM (see each chain's own confidence line for its verification path); chain C1 is HIGH. The Conclusion adds no downgrade cause of its own beyond what its cited chains already carry. This LOW band is the honest state of a diagnosis built entirely from the supplied business-context message and one external benchmark source, with none of Northbrook's own cohort, ticket, adoption, pricing, or win-loss records yet pulled — closing that gap is exactly what the recommended diagnostic wave (chain C4) exists to do, and the band should rise once wave-1 data replaces GT-10's confirmed absence.

# Northbrook Churn Spike: Root Cause and Diagnostic Plan

*First-principles analysis · 10 October 2026*

*Read with: [How to read this analysis](HOW-TO-READ.md) · [Working file](analysis-20261010T022833Z.md) · [All files](INDEX.md)*

## Executive Summary

**Recommendation:** Run the four-pronged internal diagnostic wave (renewal-cohort reconstruction, ticket-category/TTR breakdown, adoption-score audit, onboarding/TTV-by-cohort) in parallel now; gate the pricing/competitive investigation on what it shows; and do not launch a blanket intervention before wave-1 findings are in (chain C4).

**Band (from §6):** LOW

**Would change it:** Pulling renewal-cohort composition data would resolve whether the 4.1%→9.2% rise is a cohort artifact (chain C1); a ticket-category and adoption-methodology audit would test the common-upstream-cause hypothesis against the live independent-causes rival (chain C3); and confirming the five named preconditions would move the "service-decline" narrative from leading hypothesis to finding (chain C5).

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** What upstream cause or combination of causes is driving Northbrook's renewal-cohort non-renewal ratio to rise from 4.1% (Q1) to 9.2% (Q3), and — because annual contracts make any single quarter's ratio a discrete, cohort-dependent statistic rather than a continuous rate — what data must be pulled to determine whether this reported rise is a real behavioral shift, a measurement/cohort artifact, or some mix of both, before any intervention is chosen?

**Success criteria:**
1. The analysis names, for each candidate hypothesis (offer/product gaps, pricing pressure, onboarding failure, service-quality decline, competitive displacement, and composites of these), the specific data pull that would confirm or rule it out — checkable by inspecting whether section 4 names a concrete data source and discriminating observation for each.
2. The analysis determines, with explicit reasoning (not assertion), whether the two CS-flagged symptoms (ticket volume up, adoption score down) are independent causes or shared effects of one upstream event — checkable by inspecting whether section 4 contains a chain that tests this structure rather than assuming it.
3. The analysis explicitly tests whether the 4.1%→9.2% comparison is confounded by which renewal cohort fell in each quarter, rather than treating the two percentages as directly comparable — checkable by inspecting whether section 4 names the comparison's basis (same cohort size/composition or not) before drawing a conclusion from it.
4. The analysis states a most-probable root cause (or composite) with explicit inference-vs-unconfirmed labeling, and does not present any hypothesis as confirmed without data this analysis does not have — checkable by inspecting whether every causal claim in section 6 carries a confidence band and a named verification gap.
5. The analysis produces a diagnostic plan that is prioritized (not just listed) by a stated method, and intervention options sequenced by confidence and cost-of-being-wrong — checkable by inspecting whether section 4/6 shows a ranking method (not just a bullet list) and a stated sequencing rationale.

No success criterion requires selecting exactly one of leadership's five named hypotheses; a composite root cause, or a "not yet determinable without data X" verdict, satisfies these criteria as well as a single clean cause would.

---

## 2. Assumptions Table

![Assumption verdict matrix: assumption types against verdicts](report-20261010T022833Z-fig-verdicts.svg)

**Fishbone brainstorm (default six-category set — People, Process, Technology and Tools, Environment, Information, Resources) feeding the rows below.** The assumption space here is explicitly multi-causal (leadership's own five named hypotheses, stated non-exhaustive), so breadth-first brainstorming was used before challenge:

- **People:** support headcount/caseload-per-agent change; CSM turnover; account-management handoffs.
- **Process:** onboarding-process change (e.g., removed live onboarding calls); renewal-process change; escalation-path change.
- **Technology and Tools:** a product release introducing defects or removing/relocating a relied-on feature; a third-party integration breaking.
- **Environment:** a named competitor's feature or pricing move; a macro/budget-cut pressure on customers' own ops teams.
- **Information:** a change to the adoption-score formula or the feature catalog it scores, which could produce a score drop with zero behavioral change underneath; ticket-taxonomy re-categorization.
- **Resources:** a discounting or list-price change at renewal.

Each branch's discriminating observation (what would separate it from its siblings) is folded into the Verification column below rather than repeated here.

**Inversion applied to the "clean narrative."** The CS-flagged symptoms make "service-quality decline is the primary driver" feel obvious. Inverted and tested: five necessary, load-bearing preconditions for that claim are named in the Verification column of A-4 and A-12 below, and a sixth (reverse-causality — engagement decline following, not preceding, an already-made non-renewal decision) is named in A-3. All are currently unverified; this tempers the "obvious" narrative into a leading-but-unconfirmed hypothesis (carried forward as chain C5).

| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
|------------|------|-----------|---------|--------------|
| A-1: "Quarterly churn rate" is computed as (logos lost among contracts whose renewal fell due that quarter) ÷ (logos whose renewal fell due that quarter) — not a rate applied against the whole active book | untested belief | Verify the exact formula with Finance/RevOps before using the 4.1%/9.2% figures in any further math | Challenge — plausible given annual terms, but Northbrook's literal metric definition is not in evidence | unverified — flagged (feeds chain C1) |
| A-2: Annual-contract renewal dates are evenly distributed across calendar quarters (no anniversary clustering from a historical sales surge) | convention | Explicitly challenge — pull renewal-due counts by quarter, trailing 2 years | Challenge — B2B SaaS renewal books are commonly clustered around specific sales-cycle quarters; evenness should not be assumed | unverified — flagged (feeds chain C1) |
| A-3: The ticket-volume rise, the adoption-score drop, and the churn rise are timed coincidentally (not leading/lagging each other by multiple quarters, and not following an already-made non-renewal decision) | untested belief | Verify via a monthly time-series overlay of all three series, plus a reverse-causality check against lost-deal timing | Challenge — plausible but unconfirmed; the "common upstream cause" reasoning in chain C3 depends on it | unverified — flagged (feeds chain C3) |
| A-4: CS's two flagged metrics are meaningful leading indicators of churn specifically at Northbrook (not merely generically plausible signals) | untested belief | Verify via historical correlation: regress past adoption-score and ticket data against actual past churn outcomes | Challenge — no historical correlation is in evidence yet | unverified — flagged (feeds chains C3, C5) |

| A-11: A single quarter's renewal-cohort churn ratio, if held constant, approximates the true trailing-twelve-month annualized churn | untested belief (modeling assumption) | Flag explicitly as a scenario-bracketing device, not a forecast; supersede with actual trailing-12-month cohort-weighted churn once A-1/A-2 data exists | Challenge — explicitly a bracketing assumption, not a verified fact | unverified — flagged (feeds chain C2) |

| A-13: The diagnostic-prioritization trade-off's locked criteria weights and option scores reflect reasonable prioritization judgment, not a ground-truth-derived measurement | untested belief / explicitly flagged preference | Flag as analyst judgment; the flip test (chain C4) prices this assumption's failure directly | Challenge — flagged as preference per the trade-off procedure's own rule; robustness checked via flip test, not assumed away | unverified — flagged; flip-test-priced (feeds chain C4) |

---

## 3. Ground Truths

**Five-whys (reduce-to-primitives mode) applied to the headline metric before listing it as a ground truth.** Claim: "Q3 quarterly churn rate is 9.2%." Immediate constituents: (numerator) count of logos lost among contracts whose renewal fell due in Q3; (denominator) count of logos whose renewal fell due in Q3. The ratio itself (the reported 9.2%) is a verbatim-reported fact (GT-2) — it passes the irreducibility test as a *reported* figure. Its two constituents, however, are each in principle a direct measurement but are **not supplied to this analysis** and their quarter-to-quarter stability is untested (A-1, A-2, A-7) — so the parent claim is verified only as "Northbrook reported this ratio," not as "this ratio describes a stable, comparable population quarter over quarter." This decomposition is what GT-10 and chain C1 formalize.

### Dead End: Treating "ticket volume up" as fully explained by organic customer-base growth

**What was tried:** Reading the rising ticket count as simply a function of a larger or more active customer base (more seats, more integrations), with no implication of declining service quality.

**Why abandoned:** This account cannot stand alone — it does not explain the simultaneous drop in adoption scores (GT-6), and organic growth by itself does not explain a rise in the churn ratio, since growth adds new logos rather than causing existing ones to leave. Chain C3 treats "organic growth" as a possible partial contributing condition, not a complete account, because it fails the counterfactual test for the churn rise specifically.

**What it ruled out:** "Pure organic growth, no real problem" as a *complete* explanation for the combined picture (ticket volume up, adoption down, churn up). A partial contributing role for organic growth in the ticket-volume figure specifically is not ruled out and remains a candidate to quantify once ticket-rate-per-active-customer data (A-4's verification) is pulled.

### Dead End: Presenting a naive "37% annualized" figure as a confirmed crisis-level finding

**What was tried:** Directly multiplying Q3's 9.2% quarterly figure by 4 (9.2 × 4 = 36.8%) and reporting this as Northbrook's confirmed annual churn rate.

**Recommended approach:** Run the four-pronged internal diagnostic wave — renewal-cohort reconstruction, ticket-category and time-to-resolution breakdown, adoption-score audit, and onboarding/time-to-value by cohort — in parallel immediately; gate the pricing and competitive-displacement investigation on what that wave shows; and do not launch a blanket retention or discount intervention until wave-1 findings are in (chain C4).

## What's actually going on

**The headline number is less clean than it looks.** Northbrook's contracts are annual, so a "quarterly churn rate" is really the loss ratio among whichever cohort happened to be up for renewal that quarter — not a continuous rate. Nobody has pulled cohort size/composition data yet, so the 4.1%→9.2% jump is **consistent with either a real worsening or a renewal-cohort artifact** (different, smaller or larger, batch of accounts renewing in Q3 vs Q1). Published mid-market B2B SaaS benchmarks put "weak" at >12% annual logo churn. Even the *pre-spike* end of that bracket is already in weak territory — suggesting Q3 is an acceleration of an existing problem, not the onset of a new one.

**The two CS-flagged symptoms (tickets up, adoption down) are more likely two effects of one upstream cause than two separate problems.** The timing and lag structure best fit an **onboarding / time-to-value failure**: a cohort onboarded poorly ~2-3 quarters ago would generate how-to tickets and depressed adoption immediately, but wouldn't show up as churn until *that cohort's own renewal* lands — which matches a Q3 spike from an earlier onboarding breakdown. This is the leading hypothesis, not a confirmed one — a live rival is that it's two independent things (e.g., organic ticket growth from a larger customer base, plus a silent change to the adoption-score formula that mechanically dropped the score with no real behavior change).

**The "service quality decline caused churn" story, while intuitive, isn't earned yet.** Five things would all have to be true for that to hold — ticket rate *per active customer* (not raw count) is actually up; the adoption-score formula/catalog didn't change; the churned accounts are the same accounts flagged for tickets/low adoption; win-loss data doesn't point to price or a named competitor instead; and the engagement drop preceded the renewal decision rather than followed it. None of these five is currently verified.

**Run four fast, cheap internal data pulls in parallel, now:**
1. Renewal-cohort reconstruction (size/composition by quarter, actual counts not just percentages)
2. Ticket breakdown by category and time-to-resolution, normalized per active customer
3. Adoption-score methodology audit (did the formula or feature catalog change?)
4. Onboarding completion / time-to-value by cohort

**Gate the costlier investigation** (pricing/discount trends, win-loss and competitor-mention data) on what that first wave shows — it scored far lower on speed/cost in the trade-off analysis, so it's a second wave, not a parallel one.

**Guardrails:**
- Have someone outside Support/Product pull and spot-check the data — asking a team to characterize data that might implicate itself invites under-reporting.
- Don't launch a blanket retention or discount program before wave-1 lands.
- Set leadership's expectations now: because of the same annual-renewal lag that hid this problem, a correct fix won't visibly move the churn number for roughly 2-3 more quarters — don't let the next quarter's number trigger a premature "it didn't work" reversal.
- Churn won't go to zero — cross-checking against "unavoidable" attrition (company closures, M&A, budget cuts) suggests that floor is well under Northbrook's current rate, so most of this is addressable, but not all of it.

**Overall confidence: LOW** — this was built entirely from the facts given plus one external benchmark; none of Northbrook's own records have been pulled yet. That's exactly what the diagnostic wave above is for.
